claims.text: Cold spray deposition can repair or improve the damaged component surface using a hard alloy powder.
Cold spraying will produce a dense coating.
The cold-sprayed coating will adhere well to the substrate.
The cold-sprayed coating will improve wear resistance relative to both fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
The cold-sprayed coating will improve corrosion resistance relative to both fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
Cold spray repair will avoid fusion-induced hot cracking.
Cold spray will avoid the environmental and time-cost drawbacks associated with PVD and CVD.
Residual stresses and grain structure can predispose the damaged substrate to hot cracking during high-temperature processing.
Cold spray can be conducted in the solid state at temperatures below those that alter the substrate microstructure.
Optimizing particle velocity, substrate temperature, and stand-off distance can ensure proper coating formation and bonding.
The resulting coating will be mechanically interlocked with the substrate.
The resulting coating will be nanostructured and have minimal porosity.
The cold-sprayed coating will contain no fusion-induced defects.
High-velocity particle impact during cold spraying induces severe plastic deformation of the powder particles.
Severe plastic deformation produces a fine-grained, strain-hardened deposit.
High-velocity impact causes the deposit to bond acoustically to the substrate.
The fine-grained, strain-hardened deposit increases surface hardness and thereby improves wear and corrosion resistance.
Lower thermal input during cold spraying suppresses hot cracking relative to fusion welding.
Cold-sprayed repairs will have significantly greater surface hardness than both fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
The low thermal exposure of cold spraying will minimize degradation of the base-material microstructure.
